name: Rhodiola rosea
summary: A cold-climate herb (golden root) taken to fight fatigue and stress and lift mood; trials are small and conflicting, and NIH says the evidence is insufficient.
what_it_is: Rhodiola (Rhodiola rosea), also called golden root, rose root or arctic root, is a plant that grows in cold regions and at high altitudes in Europe, Asia and North America. It has a long history of traditional use in Russia, Scandinavia and other parts of Europe for work performance, endurance, fatigue, depression and altitude sickness. Today it is promoted for athletic performance, mood, thinking, energy and stress.

evidence.why: A review of 11 controlled trials found contradictory results for fatigue, all at high risk of bias or poorly reported, and NIH calls most human research low to moderate quality.

status_us.label: Dietary supplement
status_us.note: Sold as a dietary supplement. NIH notes that supplements are not approved by FDA before they are sold and that manufacturers are responsible for their safety and labeling.

benefits.claim: Less mental fatigue in 3 of 5 randomized trials and less physical fatigue in 2 of 6 trials in healthy people; every study had a high risk of bias or reporting flaws

Mixed results for depression: a 2025 review of 3 studies reported lower symptom scores, but in a 12-week placebo-controlled trial of 57 adults with mild to moderate major depression, neither rhodiola nor the antidepressant sertraline improved scores significantly more than placebo; the trial was too small to settle the question (sertraline is an approved antidepressant)

risks.risk: Dizziness, headache, trouble sleeping, and dry mouth or excess saliva
Side effects were reported by 30% of people on rhodiola versus 17% on placebo in a 12-week depression trial
Interactions with losartan, a blood pressure medicine, have been reported (NIH gives no details)
Possibly safe for up to 12 weeks; longer-term safety, and safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding, are unknown

avoid_if: Taking losartan or other blood pressure medicines (clinician first)
Depression, or taking an antidepressant (clinician first; don't stop prescribed treatment on your own)
interactions: Losartan (blood pressure medicine): interactions have been reported
Other medicines: NIH advises talking with a health care provider before using any herbal product with medicines

labs.why: No blood tests are needed; none are linked to its use.

studies.title: Rhodiola rosea for physical and mental fatigue: a systematic review
studies.people: 11 controlled trials (10 randomized) in healthy people and patients
studies.finding: Results were contradictory: 2 of 6 physical-fatigue trials and 3 of 5 mental-fatigue trials reported benefit, and all studies had a high risk of bias or reporting flaws.

studies.title: Rhodiola rosea versus sertraline for major depressive disorder: A randomized placebo-controlled trial
studies.people: 57 adults with mild to moderate major depression
studies.finding: Over 12 weeks, neither rhodiola nor sertraline lowered depression scores significantly more than placebo. Side effects were reported by 30% on rhodiola, 63% on sertraline and 17% on placebo.

studies.title: Rhodiola rosea L. reduces the depression symptoms – A systematic review
studies.people: 3 studies in people with mild to moderate depression
studies.finding: The authors conclude the extract reduced symptom severity; participant numbers and study quality were not reported in the abstract.

ask_your_clinician: Could rhodiola interact with my blood pressure medicine, antidepressant or anything else I take?
Should my fatigue or low mood be checked for an underlying cause first?
How would we judge whether it is helping?

notes_for_editor: NIH's April 2025 page says there isn't enough reliable evidence for any use and lists losartan interactions without details. The fatigue review is from 2012 and was read only as an abstract (BMC site blocked); newer fatigue and exercise trials were not reviewed. The 2025 depression review, from a Brazilian journal, is small and reports no quality ratings; it likely includes the 2015 sertraline trial. That trial was read through a Natural Medicine Journal review (the PMC copy was blocked); the reviewer favors rhodiola mainly for its lower side-effect rate, which goes beyond the trial's results. Penn Medicine's 2015 news release on the trial (NIH-funded) agrees on design and side-effect rates.
